nameStory: Clockweed gets its name from the way its delicate white flowers seem to dance and flutter in the breeze like the hands of a clock moving through time. It's also called 'beeblossom' because bees absolutely love visiting its nectar-rich flowers, and you'll often see the plant buzzing with activity during bloom time.
description: Clockweed is a graceful perennial wildflower that creates airy clouds of small white or pale pink flowers from summer into fall. The plant grows 2-4 feet tall with slender, branching stems that sway elegantly in the breeze. Originally from Texas and Louisiana, this southern beauty has found its way into New England gardens and occasionally escapes to the wild, though it's quite rare here with only 17 recorded sightings.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or pale pink flowers with four delicate petals that feel papery to the touch, each about 1/2 inch across, arranged in loose, airy clusters that dance in the slightest breeze

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, slender plant with multiple branching stems that create a graceful, vase-like shape, swaying gently and giving the whole plant an ethereal, floating appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately along the stem, with a smooth texture and slightly wavy edges that feel soft between your fingers

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, four-angled seed pods that start green and turn brown as they mature, containing tiny seeds that rattle when the dried pods are shaken

habitat: In New England, clockweed is most often found in cultivated gardens where it's grown as an ornamental plant. When it occasionally escapes cultivation, look for it in sunny, well-drained areas like field edges, roadsides, or disturbed soils. It prefers full sun and can tolerate poor, sandy soils better than rich, moist conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as slender stems with fresh green leaves, but no flowers yet - the plant is building energy for its spectacular summer show.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with clouds of white or pale pink flowers that open in the evening and attract moths and other nighttime pollinators, though they stay open during the day too.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming well into autumn until frost, while seed pods develop and mature from green to brown, eventually splitting to release seeds.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and seed heads that persist through winter, rattling in the wind.

funFact: Clockweed flowers are designed for night shift workers - they open in the evening and release their sweetest fragrance after dark to attract sphinx moths and other nocturnal pollinators, making your evening garden smell like heaven!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other evening primroses, but clockweed's distinctive airy, branched growth habit and small, delicate flowers set it apart from the larger, more robust blooms of common evening-primrose. Remember: clockweed is delicate and dancing, while evening-primrose is bold and sturdy.
contextualKnowledge: This plant has had a bit of an identity crisis - it used to be classified in the genus Gaura, which is why you'll sometimes see it called 'white gaura' or hear old-timers refer to it by that name. Scientists moved it to the evening-primrose genus (Oenothera) based on genetic studies, but many gardeners still know it by its former name.
compareHints: Unlike the bold, large yellow flowers of common evening-primrose that can be 2 inches across, clockweed has tiny, delicate white or pink flowers only half an inch wide. While common evening-primrose grows as a sturdy, upright spike, clockweed creates an airy, branching cloud that sways gracefully in the breeze. Both are in the evening-primrose family, but clockweed is much more delicate and ethereal in appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common evening-primrose is the tallest and most robust of New England's evening-primroses, with the largest flowers.
Small sundrops differs from its evening primrose relatives by staying low and sprawling rather than growing tall and upright like common evening primrose.
Among New England's evening primroses, northern evening primrose stands out for its smaller flower size compared to common evening primrose and Large-flowered evening-primrose.
Meadow evening primrose is much less common than its cousin common evening primrose, which grows much taller (3-6 feet) and has larger flowers that open in the evening.
Unlike its yellow-flowered cousin common evening-primrose which grows tall and upright, pinkladies stays low and spreads horizontally.
Unlike its evening primrose cousins that typically have four-petaled yellow flowers opening at dusk, biennial beeblossom stands out with its pink flowers and incredibly tall, airy growth habit.
Unlike the tall, upright common evening primrose with its simple oval leaves, cutleaf evening primrose stays low to the ground with deeply divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Large-flowered evening primrose stands out from other Oenothera species primarily due to its impressive flower size - much larger than common evening primrose or the various sundrops species.
Among the many evening primroses in New England, red-stalked evening primrose stands out primarily for its reddish stem coloration, while most relatives like common evening primrose have green stems.
Unlike the common evening primrose which typically grows 3-5 feet tall, tall evening primrose can reach 6 feet, making it the giant of the genus.
Bigfruit evening primrose stands out dramatically from its New England relatives like common evening primrose due to its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit rather than upright stems.
Yellow sundrops differ from common evening-primrose by blooming during the day rather than evening and having distinctive blue-green waxy leaves instead of plain green ones.
Among the evening-primroses in New England, Nodding Evening-Primrose is unique for its drooping flower buds - all other species have upright, erect buds.
